```{r setup, include = FALSE}
hasInla <- requireNamespace("INLA", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", eval = hasInla, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5,
                      out.width = "100%")
options(width = 90)
```

```{r no-inla, eval = !hasInla, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("> **INLA was not installed when this vignette was built, so the code below was not run.**\n")
```

mvrem fits **multivariate joint models** with INLA: several longitudinal markers and one or
more outcomes, each with its own family, fixed effects and random effects. An outcome is
linked to a marker through a scaled copy of the marker's linear predictor: the term
`scaled(x)` in the outcome's formula adds $\gamma \, \eta_x$ to it, with $\eta_x$ the marker's
fixed + random effects evaluated at the outcome's covariates (its time, subject, ...), and
$\gamma$ estimated. The marker and the outcome need not be measured at the same times.

The whole model is written in lme4 notation and fitted with one call, `jsm()`; INLA's
interface (stacked data, `f()` terms, copies) is built and hidden by the package.

## Installation

INLA is not on CRAN; install it first, then mvrem from GitHub (`htmlwidgets` is optional and
makes the plots interactive):

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("INLA",
                 repos = c(getOption("repos"),
                           INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"),
                 dep = TRUE)
install.packages(c("remotes", "htmlwidgets"))
remotes::install_github("LUMC/mvrem")
```

```{r library}
library(mvrem)
```

## A first model: one outcome, one marker

Simulated data, so the estimates can be compared with the truth: 100 subjects, a Gaussian
marker `x1` with a correlated random intercept and slope, measured at `t = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5`,
and a beta-distributed outcome `y` measured **between** these visits. The outcome depends on
the marker's current (error-free) value with $\gamma = 0.8$.

```{r simple-data}
set.seed(1)
n <- 100
ids <- sprintf("S%03d", seq_len(n))
dX <- data.frame(id = rep(ids, each = 4), t = rep(c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), n))         # marker visits
dY <- data.frame(id = rep(ids, each = 4), t = rep(c(0.25, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75), n))  # outcome times
z0 <- rnorm(n); z1 <- 0.6 * z0 + sqrt(1 - 0.6^2) * rnorm(n)
b0 <- 0.5 * z0; b1 <- 0.2 * z1                # random intercept (SD 0.5), slope (SD 0.2), cor 0.6
eta <- function(d) { i <- match(d$id, ids); 1 + 0.5 * d$t + b0[i] + b1[i] * d$t }
dX$x1 <- eta(dX) + rnorm(nrow(dX), sd = 0.2)                    # marker
mu <- plogis(-1 + 0.8 * eta(dY))                               # gamma = 0.8
dY$y <- rbeta(nrow(dY), 20 * mu, 20 * (1 - mu))                # outcome, phi = 20
dY$y[sample(nrow(dY), 60)] <- NA                               # missing outcomes are predicted
head(dY, 3)
head(dX, 3)
```

### The model

All formulae go in one list. A formula with a `scaled()` term is an outcome, one without is
a marker. Random effects are written as in lme4, `(1 + t | id)`, or with `re()` to set their
prior; here the Wishart prior of the block is centred on an lme4 fit of the marker
(`scale = "data"`). The data are given per response; families default to Gaussian.

```{r simple-model}
m <- jsm(
  list(y  ~ 1 + t + scaled(x1),
       x1 ~ 1 + t + re(1 + t | id, prior = wishartPrec(scale = "data"))),
  data   = list(y = dY, x1 = dX),
  family = list(y = betaFamily()),
  criteria = TRUE                     # DIC, WAIC and CPO for modelFit()
)
summary(m)
```

True values: $\gamma = 0.8$, $\phi = 20$; `y` intercept $-1$, no effect of `t`; `x1`
intercept 1, slope 0.5, SDs 0.5 and 0.2, correlation 0.6, residual SD 0.2.

### Results

`estimatesTable()` collects all estimates (fixed effects, associations, SDs and correlations,
family parameters) in one table; `format(..., "markdown")` or `"latex"` writes it for a
report.

```{r simple-estimates, results = "asis"}
cat(format(estimatesTable(m), "markdown", digits = 2))
```

`plot()` shows the data of each equation, one line per subject, and after the fit the fitted
values (open circles: predictions of the missing outcomes). With htmlwidgets installed the
plot is interactive: hovering a subject highlights it in all panels, a click pins it.

```{r simple-plot}
plot(m)
```

Further accessors: `fixedEffects()`, `associations()`, `hyperparameters()`,
`randomEffects()`, `varianceComponents()` (SDs and correlations rather than INLA's
precisions), `fittedValues()`, `residuals()` and `modelFit()`:

```{r simple-var}
varianceComponents(m)
modelFit(m)
```

and plots of them: `plotFixedEffects()`, `plotAssociations()`, `plotRandomEffects()`,
`plotVarianceComponents()`, `plotResiduals()`.

```{r simple-ranef, fig.height = 4}
plotRandomEffects(m, type = "pairs")
```

### Predictions

`predict()` gives the posterior of the fitted mean at new rows: new subjects (random effects
from their distribution) or new times of known subjects (their own random effects).

```{r simple-predict}
new <- data.frame(id = rep(c("S001", "S002", "new"), each = 5),
                  t  = rep(seq(0, 2, by = 0.5), 3))
p <- predict(m, new)
head(p, 3)
plot(p)
```

### The model in a picture and in equations

```{r simple-diagram, fig.height = 2.6}
plotModel(m)
```

`latexEquation()` writes the model as LaTeX; with `annotate = "tooltip"` hovering a symbol
shows its estimate (`"inline"` writes the estimates under the symbols).

```{r simple-equation, results = "asis"}
cat(format(latexEquation(m, annotate = "tooltip"), delim = "$$"))
```

## Several outcomes and markers of different types

Each response has its own family; family inputs follow the response after `|`:
`trials(n)` for binomial, `exposure(pt)` for Poisson, `event(status)` for survival and
`weights(w)` for observation weights. An outcome may be linked to several markers, and
arguments of `scaled()` set the prior of its coefficient.

```{r moderate-data}
set.seed(2)
n <- 120
d <- data.frame(id = sprintf("S%03d", rep(seq_len(n), each = 5)), t = rep(0:4 / 2, n))
u <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n)[as.integer(factor(d$id)), ]
etaX <- 1 + 0.5 * d$t + 0.5 * u[, 1] + 0.2 * u[, 2] * d$t          # Gaussian marker x1
etaC <- 0.5 + 0.2 * d$t + 0.5 * u[, 3]                              # count marker (log rate)
d$x1 <- etaX + rnorm(nrow(d), sd = 0.3)
d$pt <- runif(nrow(d), 0.8, 1.2)
d$cnt <- rpois(nrow(d), d$pt * exp(etaC))
muY <- plogis(-1 + 0.3 * d$t + 0.6 * (etaX - 1) + 0.3 * (etaC - 0.5))
d$y <- rbeta(nrow(d), 30 * muY, 30 * (1 - muY))
d$n <- 10
d$k <- rbinom(nrow(d), d$n, pnorm(-0.3 + 0.5 * (etaX - 1)))
```

```{r moderate-model}
m2 <- jsm(
  list(y ~ 1 + t + scaled(x1, prior = normalCoef(0, 1)) + scaled(cnt),
       k | trials(n) ~ 1 + t + scaled(x1),
       x1 ~ 1 + t + re(1 + t | id, prior = wishartPrec(scale = "data")),
       cnt | exposure(pt) ~ 1 + t + (1 | id)),
  data   = d,
  family = list(y = betaFamily(), k = binomialFamily(link = "probit"), cnt = "poisson")
)
associations(m2)
```

True values: $\gamma_{y,x_1} = 0.6$, $\gamma_{y,\mathit{cnt}} = 0.3$, $\gamma_{k,x_1} = 0.5$.

```{r moderate-diagram, fig.height = 3.5}
plotModel(m2)
```

## A survival outcome

A time to event with right censoring is written `time | event(status) ~ ...` with
`weibullSurvFamily()` or `exponentialSurvFamily()`, one row per subject. The marker enters the
hazard at the covariate values of the survival row: `t = 0` below, the subject's marker level
at baseline. The two parts have their own data frames.

```{r survival}
set.seed(6)
n <- 200
b0 <- rnorm(n, sd = 0.5); b1 <- rnorm(n, sd = 0.25)
etaS <- function(i, t) 1 + 0.4 * t + b0[i] + b1[i] * t
T <- (-log(runif(n)) / exp(-2.5 + 0.8 * etaS(seq_len(n), 0)))^(1 / 1.5)  # Weibull, alpha 1.5
C <- runif(n, 1, 4)
dSurv <- data.frame(id = sprintf("S%03d", seq_len(n)), time = pmin(T, C),
                    status = as.integer(T <= C), t = 0)
dMark <- data.frame(id = rep(dSurv$id, each = 5), t = rep(c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2), n))
dMark$x1 <- etaS(rep(seq_len(n), each = 5), dMark$t) + rnorm(nrow(dMark), sd = 0.2)
dMark <- dMark[dMark$t <= rep(dSurv$time, each = 5), ]               # visits before the event

m3 <- jsm(
  list(time | event(status) ~ 1 + scaled(x1),
       x1 ~ 1 + t + (1 + t || id)),
  dataOut = dSurv, dataLong = dMark,
  family  = list(time = weibullSurvFamily())
)
estimatesTable(m3)
```

True values: $\gamma = 0.8$ (a log hazard ratio per unit of the marker), Weibull shape
$\alpha = 1.5$.

`plot()` draws the survival outcome against its own time: the Kaplan-Meier curve (censored
times as open circles) and the model's survival curve averaged over the subjects. A fit with
`inlaOptions = list(control.compute = list(config = TRUE))` adds a 95% band from posterior draws;
`survivalCurves()` gives the curves as a data frame.

```{r survival-plot}
plot(m3)
```

## Several cores, several fits

INLA uses all cores of the machine for one fit by default. `jsm(threads = )` changes that:
a number, `"auto"` (the cores `availableThreads()` finds: it respects container limits,
SLURM / SGE allocations and `R CMD check`, and on Apple Silicon counts only the performance
cores) or `"A:B"` (outer : inner INLA threads). `refit()` and `predict()` take it too.

```{r threads}
availableThreads()
```

Independent fits (candidate models, simulation replicates, predictions by refitting) run in
parallel with `jsmApply()`, which divides the core budget among its workers. Here the first
model with and without the data-centred prior of the random-effect block:

```{r apply}
variants <- list(
  "wishartPrec(scale = \"data\")" = x1 ~ 1 + t + re(1 + t | id, prior = wishartPrec(scale = "data")),
  "INLA's default prior"          = x1 ~ 1 + t + (1 + t | id))
gammas <- jsmApply(variants, function(fx) {
  fit <- jsm(list(y ~ 1 + t + scaled(x1), fx), data = list(y = dY, x1 = dX),
             family = list(y = betaFamily()))
  associations(fit)[, c("mean", "q0.025", "q0.975")]   # return a table, not the model
})
do.call(rbind, gammas)
```

On a 16-core cluster node, four candidate models ran about twice as fast this way as one
after another, and simulation studies (many fits of the same model) three to four times as
fast; on a laptop, where INLA already keeps the cores busy within one fit, the gain is
smaller. Workers are forked copies of the R session on Linux and macOS (in a terminal or
`Rscript`); on Windows and in RStudio they are separate R sessions, which load the installed
mvrem and receive the variables `FUN` uses. Every worker holds its own fit in memory.

## Overview

| Function | Gives |
|---|---|
| `jsm(form, data, family)` | build and fit the model (`fit = FALSE`: build only) |
| `summary()`, `estimatesTable()` | all estimates, readable names |
| `fixedEffects()`, `associations()`, `hyperparameters()`, `coef()` | posterior summaries |
| `randomEffects()`, `varianceComponents()` | subject effects; SDs, correlations, covariance matrices |
| `fittedValues()`, `residuals()`, `modelFit()` | fitted means, residuals; DIC, WAIC, log score |
| `predict(m, newdata)` | posterior of the mean at new rows; `plot()` of the result |
| `plot()`, `plotResiduals()`, `plotRandomEffects()`, `plotVarianceComponents()`, `plotFixedEffects()`, `plotAssociations()` | data and fitted values; diagnostics; posteriors |
| `plotModel()`, `latexEquation()` | diagram and equations of the model |
| `update()`, `refit()` | re-run with changed arguments / INLA options |
| `inlaFormula()`, `inlaData()`, `inlaArguments()`, `inlaFit()`, `formatInlaFormula()` | what was given to INLA, and its result |

Families: `gaussianFamily()`, `studentTFamily()`, `lognormalFamily()`, `gammaFamily()`,
`betaFamily()`, `poissonFamily()`, `negBinomialFamily()`, `binomialFamily()`,
`betaBinomialFamily()`, zero-inflated Poisson and negative binomial, `weibullSurvFamily()`,
`exponentialSurvFamily()` and `inlaFamily()` for any other INLA likelihood. Priors:
`gammaPrec()`, `pcSd()`, `halfNormalSd()`, `halfCauchySd()` (also scaled from the data),
`wishartPrec()` for correlated blocks and `normalCoef()` for associations. See their help pages
for details.
